Some readers keep a book on a shelf as a possession; this one treats rereading as a ritual of return. Every few years, when the world has rearranged itself enough, they open the same pages again. The cover is familiar, the margins crowded with old reactions, but the book seems to have changed because they have. They notice sentences they once skimmed, arguments that now feel sharper or stranger, and characters whose choices once seemed obvious but now reveal hesitation, luck, or privilege.

The first reread is often an act of repair: a return to a former self, to a period when the book had seemed capable of explaining everything. Later revisits are less certain. The reader no longer asks only what the book meant then; they ask what it means now, whether its wisdom has survived, and whether their admiration has been built on a youthful misreading. They may argue with it silently, underline a different passage, or skip a chapter that once mattered.

Rereading does not make the book fixed. It makes the reader visible. Each return exposes the distance between who they were and who they have become, while also suggesting that memory is another kind of fiction: selective, revisable, and dependent on where we happen to stand. By the final page, they close the book not because they have finished it, but because they have finished another version of themselves.
